problems.description: Session-1 'greenfield' commit discards the entire provided Tier 2 seed (SQLite, Blueprints, JWT auth, multi-file structure) instead of building on it — near-zero reuse of the seeded baseline, the rewrite/flail behavior the story instrumentation exists to measure.

Flat JSON-file persistence guarded only by a threading.Lock is per-process; concurrent or multi-worker request handling can interleave writes/corrupt state — a regression versus the seed's transactional SQLite store.

Half-migration: post-commit files celery_config.py, notifications.py, repositories.py (old modular architecture) coexist with a flat single-file app.py, leaving stale modules with no role in the new design.

Convention score 0.73 with 8 unresolved violations across app.py, celery_config.py, notifications.py, repositories.py, test_app.py (PascalCase classes, snake_case functions, UPPER_CASE module constants).

test_app.py survives while the auth API surface it targeted was deleted; the retained suite likely no longer matches the rewritten app (test_executed_success not verifiable from this diff — flagged as inference).

strengths: SonarQube delta is positive for cleanliness: +0 bugs, -3 smells, +0.0% duplication on a -240-line rewrite.
Coherent, dramatically simpler design; the docstring explicitly documents the flat-file 'no database' storage decision.
Uses timezone-aware datetimes (datetime, timezone) rather than the seed's naive utcnow() timestamps.
commit_reviews.summary: Session 1 rewrote the provided SQLite/Blueprint seed into a flat single-file JSON task API, yielding cleaner-by-SonarQube code but discarding the seeded architecture and swapping transactional storage for a process-local flat file — worse for the multi-session story baseline it was meant to extend.

problems.description: Hand-rolled JWT (base64 + hmac) instead of a vetted library like PyJWT/flask-jwt-extended; custom crypto in auth paths is a well-known source of subtle vulnerabilities and adds long-term maintenance burden.
Hardcoded fallback secret 'development-secret-change-me' means tokens are forgeable whenever JWT_SECRET_KEY is unset.
Cognitive complexity +27 is concentrated in the auth path (_current_user's long try/except decoding chain), making the token-validation logic harder to follow and test.

Convention violations in the touched files (app.py, test_app.py: PascalCase/constant-case); note the 0.73 score is dragged down by violations in untouched files (celery_config.py, notifications.py, repositories.py).
test_app.py was updated, but JWT expiry, signature-tampering, and owner-isolation edge cases would benefit from explicit coverage (test diff truncated, so this is unverified).

strengths: Respects the explicit flat-file storage constraint — users live in the same JSON store, no database, +0 new files.
Backward-compatible migration backfills owner_id for pre-auth data files instead of breaking them.
Sound crypto hygiene where it could have been lazy: hmac.compare_digest constant-time comparison and werkzeug password hashing.
Consistent owner_id scoping applied across create/list/get/update task routes.
Idiomatic Flask auth decorator with g.user; existing route/storage patterns preserved.
commit_reviews.summary: A substantial, well-scoped feature that fits the flat-file architecture and cleanly migrates existing data, but hand-rolled JWT plus a hardcoded fallback secret introduce real security/maintainability debt — and the 0.73 convention score mostly reflects violations in files this diff did not touch.

problems.description: Celery + Redis broker is wired for a mock print-only email task with no worker consuming the notifications queue — the background job never actually executes unless a separate worker is started, over-engineering the current behavior.

app.py imports notifications at module top-level, coupling the Flask app to the Celery task (and transitively celery_config + broker) at import time, so the app fails to start if Celery is not installed.

previous_status is read inside _file_lock but the transition decision fires outside it; under concurrent PUTs the completed-transition check can double-send or miss (race window between read and dispatch).
A fresh tasks.json seed (empty users/tasks) is committed, discarding any prior runtime state from earlier sessions.

Most of the 8 flagged convention violations are pre-existing or analyzer false positives — +0 classes were added (the 'PascalCase' flags fire on instances like app/celery_app), and repositories.py is untouched by this diff; the 0.73 mechanical score overstates this commit's own debt.

strengths: Transition-only notification logic correctly guards against double-firing on repeated 'completed' PUTs, and is covered by a dedicated test.
Dispatch is issued after _write_data and outside the file lock, so the broker call never blocks the storage critical section.
Idiomatic Celery setup: explicit task name, task_routes queue mapping, env-configurable broker URL; tests assert broker + route config.
Follows existing patterns: reuses the auth_client fixture and monkeypatch style, snake_case naming, module docstrings, and the register endpoint's validation/error shape.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, well-tested integration session that adds Celery-backed completion notifications consistent with the codebase's existing structure, at the cost of a slightly over-engineered mock task and a small notification race outside the file lock.

problems.description: New repositories.py flags module-level constants that should be UPPER_CASE (one of the 8 measured violations introduced by this commit; the app.py/celery_config.py/notifications.py/test_app.py violations are pre-existing outside this diff).

_repositories() constructs two fresh repository objects on every request; the repositories carry no per-request state (they take DATA_FILE and _file_lock), so a module-level instance would suffice — current shape adds pointless allocation and invites misuse.

The legacy migration block in _read_data() (backfilling owner_id for pre-auth files) is removed from app.py; correctness now depends on repositories.py preserving that path — verify before trusting old data files.

strengths: Clean repository-layer extraction isolates all flat-file I/O (read/write/atomic tmp+fsync) from request handlers, which now express intent via find_by_username/create_for_user/get_for_user.
Net -102 lines and -13 inline storage accesses with zero new bugs and zero new smells per SonarQube, and cognitive complexity only +3 despite +18 functions/+3 classes.
Respects the explicit flat-file no-database requirement (docstring kept) and the existing auth/werkzeug patterns.
commit_reviews.summary: Architecturally sound refactor that cleanly extracts the flat-file storage layer into UserRepository/TaskRepository with no new bugs or smells, sitting at the measured 0.73 convention score solely on UPPER_CASE/class-name nits (one newly introduced, the rest pre-existing).

problems.description: paginate_for_user materializes and sorts the full user task list in memory before slicing (O(n) per request, total requires the full scan); consistent with the existing list_for_user pattern but the 'cursor' is really an index lookup over a snapshot, so it will not scale and can drift if tasks are inserted/deleted between pages.

Adds a flask_limiter + Redis storage dependency (redis://localhost:6379/1) but the diff shows no requirements.txt change; verify the package is pinned so fresh deploys don't break. in_memory_fallback_enabled=true mitigates the hard Redis coupling.

SonarQube reports cognitive complexity +15: the list_tasks handler now bundles cursor parsing, limit validation, envelope shaping, and error branches — extraction of the pagination-param parsing into a helper would reduce it.

The shared 100/min default limit applies to every route including /auth/login and /auth/register, so heavy API use consumes the same budget as brute-force attempts; route-specific or stricter auth limits would be more defensive. The per-request _current_user() DB lookup in _rate_limit_key also adds a query to every request.

test_rate_limit_returns_retry_after performs 100 sequential login round-trips to exhaust the budget — functionally correct and well-asserted (Retry-After + body), but slow; the shared 100/min global budget makes the test costly to maintain.

Measured convention score 0.73 reflects 8 pre-existing naming violations (PascalCase classes, UPPER_CASE constants in celery_config.py/notifications.py/repositories.py/test_app.py); this commit introduces no new violations — all added functions (_rate_limit_key, rate_limit_exceeded, paginate_for_user) are snake_case and no new classes were added.

strengths: Rate limiting keyed by authenticated user id with IP fallback is sound security design, and the custom 429 handler correctly propagates Retry-After.
Pagination parameter validation is thorough (limit bounds 1-100, invalid cursor/limit -> 400, stale cursor -> explicit 'cursor not found'), with an informative {data, next_cursor, total} envelope.

Respects existing layering: pagination lives in the repository alongside list_for_user/get_for_user, the handler owns request parsing, and tests were updated for the new shape plus new coverage for pagination and rate limiting.
Good test hygiene: limiter.reset() in the fixture isolates rate-limit state between tests, and in_memory_fallback_enabled keeps the app functional if Redis is unavailable.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured cross-cutting commit that adds rate limiting and cursor pagination with strong validation and updated tests, respecting existing repository/Flask patterns — the measured 0.73 convention score reflects pre-existing naming violations rather than new ones, while minor scalability and dependency-pinning concerns apply.

compounding_issues: Session 1's flat-file JSON store (single thread Lock, whole-file atomic rewrite per mutation) became a fixed constraint: session 5's cursor pagination must re-sort the user's full task list in memory on every GET /tasks, with no index to lean on.
Session 2 hand-rolled the HS256 JWT (base64url/hmac by hand, no PyJWT) and it was retained through every later session — a standing custom-crypto surface that never got hardened or replaced.

Redis dependencies accumulated across sessions (Celery broker on 6379/0 in session 3, Flask-Limiter storage on 6379/1 in session 5) and leaked shared state into the test suite, causing the session-5 rate-limit test to flake (9 errors + 2 failures before the fixture was patched with limiter.reset()).
Binary __pycache__/*.pyc artifacts were committed from session 3 onward and never cleaned up — repo hygiene debt that persisted to the final commit.
key_decisions: Session 1 (greenfield): complete rewrite away from the seed's SQLite/Blueprint/items/admin architecture into a focused JSON flat-file task API with atomic mkstemp+os.replace writes and a thread lock — re-scoping the whole product.
Session 2 (feature_addition): added auth via hand-rolled HS256 JWTs, werkzeug password hashing, and owner-scoped task access (owner_id) with backward-compatible storage migration for pre-auth data.

Session 3 (integration): wired Celery/Redis background notification emails with a routed 'notifications' queue, fired only on a genuine pending->completed transition, plus an email field on registration.
Session 4 (refactor): extracted repositories.py (BaseRepository ABC + UserRepository/TaskRepository), centralizing all data access behind a seam that session 5 then extended with paginate_for_user.
Session 5 (cross_cutting): added cursor pagination with limit/cursor validation and Redis-backed Flask-Limiter rate limiting keyed by user (authenticated) or IP (anonymous), with a JSON 429 handler.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across the five sessions. The story moves from an unauthenticated, minimal task store (session 1, ~5 tests) through a full auth layer (session 2), a Celery/Redis notification integration (session 3), a structural refactor that slimmed app.py by extracting repositories.py (session 4), and finally cross-cutting hardening in cursor pagination plus rate limiting (session 5, 14 passing tests). The code is test-driven at every step — the test suite grew monotonically (5→8→11→14) and was verified green at the final commit. The only turbulence was session 5's own debugging, where the newly introduced Redis-backed rate limiter broke shared test state and produced a flurry of errors/failures that the agent diagnosed and fixed by resetting the limiter in the test fixture. Structurally, session 5 lands cleanly because session 4 deliberately created the repository seam it needed; the flat-file storage and hand-rolled JWT decisions made early are the main technical debts carried through the whole arc.
story_review.summary: A well-orchestrated, test-driven progression from a bare flat-file task API to a hardened, authenticated, paginated, rate-limited service — coherent phases that build on each other — though early choices (flat-file store, hand-rolled JWT, and accumulating Redis state) left compounding technical debt.
